content.subtitle: Overview ℹ️
content.description: Agile methodologies are the latest view of systems development that emerged out of the object-oriented approach. They are considered one of the easiest and most uncomplicated routes to transform an idea and varied needs into feasible software solutions. The agile method is an iterative and incremental tactic for software design. It utilises constant planning, understanding, upgrading, team partnership, development, and delivery. The process is fragmented into separate models, which encourages flexibility to changes. Errors are resolved in the intermediate stage of the project because the development process is iterative. This helps the final deliverable product to better match the customer’s wants, resulting in systems that are user-friendly. In February 2001, proponents of alternative approaches met in Utah and reached a consensus on underlying principles, resulting in “The Agile Manifesto”. Agile software development is a lightweight approach proposed to overcome limitations of other development methods and to reduce overhead and cost while providing flexibility to adopt requirement changes at any stage. Agile methodologies form a distinct category of software development methodologies. Their common goal is being “adaptive” rather than “predictive”. Generally, they consider "upfront" documentation, modelling, and design as a waste of time. This is managed through a certain set of values and principles. Agile is a conceptual framework for software engineering. It begins with a starting planning phase and follows an iterative and incremental approach throughout the project lifecycle. The initial goal is to reduce overhead and adopt changes without excessive rework or risking the process. Agile methods are processes that support the agile philosophy, which includes agile values and principles. The agile methodologies share three key principles: a focus on adaptive rather than predictive methodologies, a focus on people rather than roles, and a self-adaptive process. All agile development methodologies are based on the agile manifesto and a set of twelve principles. The manifesto emphasises focusing developers on their working conditions, working software, customers, and addressing changing requirements, instead of detailed processes, tools, comprehensive documentation, contracts, and detailed plans. Each Agile method consists of a different combination of practices, which describe how day-to-day work is done. Methods differ by choosing their appropriate terminology and practices. Agile methodologies are typically based only on the twelve principles of agile software. These principles include:

items.definition: Software is delivered early and continuously, satisfying the customer. 🚀
Being open to changes in requirements even late in the project. 🔄
Delivering completed work at regular intervals, preferably short ones. ⏰
Customers and developers work together to solve the business problem. 🤝
Assembling a motivated team, providing support, and trusting them. 💪
Communicating face-to-face regularly. This is the most efficient and effective method of gathering requirements within the development team. 🗣️
Using completed work to measure progress. The primary measure is working, executing software. 📊
Creating processes that promote sustainable efforts and a constant pace of work. This means a level of work that can be maintained indefinitely without worker burnout. ⚖️
Agility is heightened through attention to both technical excellence and good design. 🛠️
Encouraging simplicity, the avoidance of unnecessary work, is essential. ✂️
Recognising that the best work emerges from self-organized teams that deliver the best architectures and designs. 🌟
Reflecting regularly on how the development team can be more effective and fine-tuning their approach. 🔍

content.subtitle: Agility Definition 🏃‍♂️
content.description: Agility is defined as the ability to rapidly change body direction, accelerate, or decelerate, influenced by balance, strength, coordination, and skill level. It can be improved by developing an adequate base of strength and conditioning. In the context of systems development, agility refers to the ability to adapt quickly to changing circumstances and make decisions efficiently.

items.definition: Responding quickly to market changes, customer demands, or external factors through efficient processes, flexible systems, and a responsive workforce. Important in rapidly changing industries.

Anticipating and responding to changes in the competitive landscape, industry trends, or long-term factors with a clear vision, flexible strategy, and quick decision-making. Important for staying ahead.
Leaders adapting to changing circumstances and leading effectively, involving communication, quick decisions, and strong relationships. Important for responding quickly to changing market conditions.

Teams working effectively together and adapting quickly to changing circumstances, involving a shared vision, clear communication, collaboration, and problem-solving. Important for responding quickly to customer demands and changing market conditions.
An individual's ability to learn quickly and adapt to new situations through openness to new experiences, seeking feedback, and continuous skill development. Important for staying up-to-date.

An individual's ability to regulate emotions and adapt to changing circumstances, involving managing stress, effective communication, and building relationships. Important for creating a positive work environment.

An organization's ability to quickly adapt to changes in the market, customer demands, or other external factors, involving flexibility to respond to opportunities and challenges. Important for responding quickly to market conditions and customer demands. The Framework for Business Agility (FBA) includes Culture, Leadership, and Collaboration.

An organization's ability to quickly adapt across the entire organization. It involves a culture of agility and collaboration across all departments and levels. Important for responding quickly and efficiently while maintaining customer satisfaction and employee engagement.

content.subtitle: Evolution of Agile 🕰️
content.description: The evolution of Agile methodologies traces back to the 1990s as a response to slow, inflexible traditional methods. Early influences included iterative and incremental development (RAD, Spiral model) and Lean manufacturing principles (eliminating waste, optimising value). The Manifesto for Agile Software Development in 2001 was a pivotal moment. It outlined core values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. Scrum was introduced in the mid-1990s. It emphasises iterative development with small, cross-functional teams working in short cycles called sprints to deliver potentially shippable increments. It includes roles (Scrum Master, Product Owner), artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog), and ceremonies (Sprint Planning, Daily Stand-ups). Extreme Programming (XP), developed in the late 1990s, is another influential method. It emphasises practices like test-driven development (TDD), pair programming, continuous integration, and frequent releases. XP focuses on high-quality software and adapting to changes through feedback and communication. Since the early 2000s, Agile methodologies have continued to evolve and expand. Various frameworks have emerged, including Kanban, Lean software development, and Development operations. The evolution of Agile methodologies is characterised by a shift towards lightweight, adaptive approaches focused on delivering value quickly and responding to change effectively. Agile has become the dominant paradigm not only in software development but also in other domains and industries.

items.definition: Originating from Japanese for "visual board" or "signboard", connected to "just in time". Initially lean manufacturing, it moved to software development. It uses visual methods (Kanban Board with columns) to manage projects, increasing visibility and helping teams prepare for upcoming tasks to deliver "just in time". Requires interaction and transparency.

One of the most popular agile methodologies. It breaks down phases into cycles called 'sprints'. Development time for each sprint is maximised and dedicated, managing one sprint at a time. It focuses on continuous deliverables and allows adjusting priorities. Scrum Team has exclusive roles like scrum master and product owner with daily communication.

Founded on four core values: communication, simplicity, feedback, and courage. Focuses on constant development and customer satisfaction. Uses sprints or short development cycles. Very supportive of constant and varying customer demands, encouraging developers to accept changes even late. Project is tested from initial stages by collecting feedback.

A group of smaller methodologies (Crystal Yellow, Clear, Red, Orange) by Alistair Cockburn. Each has a unique framework based on system criticality (Comfort, Essential Money, Discretionary Money, Life), team size, and project priorities. Addresses prompt delivery, regularity, less administration, high user involvement, and customer satisfaction. Advocates that each project is unique and needs diverse practices, processes, and policies. Considered one of the most lightweight methods.

Developed to address the need for a standard industry charter for swift software delivery. Gives a comprehensive structure for planning, executing, managing, and scaling software development. Based on a business-driven approach and eight principles. Believes modifications are always expected, and quality and timely delivery must never be negotiated.

Iterative, customer-centric, and incremental method incorporating best practices. Primary goal is to consistently produce working software in a timely fashion. Lifecycle stages include developing an overall model, creating feature lists, planning by feature, designing by feature, and building by feature. Suitable for large project teams.

Based on seven principles: deleting what doesn’t matter (waste removal), quality development (control residuals), knowledge creation (document infrastructure), defer commitments (understand requirements first), delivery promptly (value quickly), respecting the team (communication, conflict management), and optimising the whole (perfecting sequence, removing errors). Optimizes development time and resources. Easily scalable and adaptable.

A set of workflow and organizational patterns for implementing agile practices at an enterprise scale. Allows taking advantage of a relatively light framework while maintaining centralized decision-making for efficiency. Applies the agile philosophy to software executives addressing strategic issues.

content.subtitle: Simplicity in Agile ✂️
content.description: Choosing the right agile methodology requires a dynamic approach, considering advantages and disadvantages to entice talent and convey remarkable digital experiences. Simplicity in Agile is about doing exemplary work, eliminating unnecessary complexities, and focusing on what truly matters. Prioritization is key. Simplicity is a fundamental principle. It is integrated through:

items.definition: Advocating for 'just enough' documentation upfront and iterating based on feedback. Prevents wasting effort on unnecessary details.

Building software incrementally in small, manageable chunks (iterations/sprints). Each iteration delivers a working, usable subset. Breaks work into smaller pieces for effective prioritization and more frequent value delivery.

Regularly restructuring code without changing external behaviour to improve readability, maintainability, and efficiency. Keeps codebase clean and simple, reduces technical debt, and allows easier adaptation to changes.
Writing tests before code. Encourages simplicity by focusing on desired behaviour. Guides developers to write only necessary code, resulting in simpler implementations.

Emphasising feedback from stakeholders, customers, and team members. Helps identify opportunities to simplify the product, remove unnecessary features, and prioritize effectively based on changing requirements and market conditions.

Empowering self-organizing teams to make decisions and adapt processes. Allows teams to simplify workflows, eliminate bottlenecks, and optimise for efficiency. Trusts teams to find the simplest solutions.

content.subtitle: Tools and Techniques 🧰
content.description: Overall, simplicity in Agile prioritizes value, minimises waste, and continuously seeks efficient ways of working. By embracing simplicity, Agile teams can deliver high-quality software while maintaining flexibility and adaptability. Agility can be achieved through various tools and techniques. Some tools mentioned are: Agile Methodologies, Design Thinking, Development Operations, Lean Startup, Cloud Computing, Continuous Improvement, Cynefin Framework, and SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework).

items.definition: Adopting agility requires a shift in mindset, culture, and behaviour, necessitating training for employees.
Implementing Agile processes may require changes like adopting new tools, revising workflows, and modifying communication channels.
Adopting agility requires a cultural shift towards collaboration, transparency, and continuous improvement, potentially requiring changes to culture, leadership, and management.
Focus on iterative/incremental development and continuous integration/delivery enables faster product/service delivery.
Emphasis on continuous improvement, collaboration, and feedback leads to higher quality.
Faster, more efficient delivery of high-quality products/services increases customer satisfaction and loyalty.
Fosters experimentation, learning, and continuous improvement, leading to increased innovation and creativity.
Faster and more efficient delivery reduces costs associated with delays, rework, and wasted effort.
Becoming more responsive to market changes, customer needs, and competitive pressures provides a competitive advantage.

content.subtitle: Criticisms of Agile 🚫
content.description: Agility is a versatile and powerful approach requiring a shift in mindset, culture, and behaviour, not just implementing processes and tools. Agile methodologies also have critics.

items.definition: A major criticism is that the requirement for co-location of the development team seems unrealistic given today's business environment with offshoring, outsourcing, and subcontracting.
Another criticism is that if not carefully managed, it can devolve into a prototyping approach ("programmers gone wild") where solutions are hacked together.

A third criticism, based on the lack of actual documentation, raises issues regarding the auditability of systems. Without sufficient documentation, neither the system nor the development process can be assured.
A fourth criticism questions whether agile approaches can deliver large mission-critical systems.

content.subtitle: Overview ℹ️
content.description: Scrum is the most popular Agile framework due to its flexibility and adaptability to any team size or project. One prime benefit is that work is done concurrently by the development team rather than chronologically. Scrum facilitates collaboration between teams working on complex projects and products. Scrum helps teams learn from experiences, organise themselves while handling issues, and reflect on successes/failures to improve. It groups tasks into columns based on progress. Scrum usually breaks down a project into sprints, planning and managing one sprint at a time. Scrum also has unique project roles: a scrum master and Product Owner.

content.subtitle: Scrum Practices ⚙️
content.description: Practices that distinguish Scrum from other approaches include:

items.definition: The team organises work in short cycles.
Management doesn’t interrupt the team during a work cycle.
The team reports to the client, not to the manager.
The team estimates how much time and effort work will take.
The team decides how much work it can do in an iteration.
The team decides how to do the iteration’s work.
The team measures its own performance.
The team defines work goals before each cycle.
Work and desired outcomes are defined through a progressively refined description called the Product Backlog.
The team works to systematically and continuously improve and to remove impediments.
The Product Owner (PO) is the liaison between customers and the development team and champion for the product. Ensures product expectations are communicated and agreed upon.

The Development Team (DT) works together to develop and test incremental releases. They are champions for sustainable development practices. Scrum teams are usually 5-9 members, tight-knit and co-located. (Note: Source later states 5-7 members).

The Scrum Master (SM) is the champion of Scrum within the team. Primary responsibility is to ensure best scrum practices. Schedules needed resources for sprint planning, stand-up, sprint review, and sprint retrospective.

content.subtitle: How Scrum Works 🔄
content.description: How Does Scrum Work? It has the following steps/activities:

items.definition: A list of tasks the team must complete to achieve stakeholders’ goals.
Selected tasks from the product backlog are chosen for teams to focus on and deliver during the sprint.
Tasks discussed in the previous phase are added to the sprint backlog.
Usually a team of 5-9 members working on sprint backlog tasks. (Note: Source later states 5-7 members).

Daily 15-minute meetings for team members to synchronise activities, report bottlenecks, and plan for the next 24 hours. Also called 'daily stand-up'. The motive is to keep team members in exact alignment. Team members often focus on three questions: What did I do yesterday? What do I plan to do today? Are there any obstacles?

Held after the sprint is completed. Attended by the product owner, scrum master, stakeholders, and the scrum team. The team discusses accomplishments and receives feedback/suggestions. The product owner presents the backlog’s top items to stakeholders for feedback on upcoming sprints.
Follows the sprint review. The team identifies potential mistakes/issues and ways to handle them. Data from this stage is incorporated into planning the next sprint.
Stakeholders receive a workable and usable output.

content.subtitle: Professional Scrum 🏆
content.description: Professional Scrum is a framework by Scrum.org (founded by Ken Schwaber) for implementing Agile principles and practices. It provides guidelines for applying Scrum effectively in various contexts, emphasizing professionalism, empiricism, and continuous improvement. Professional Scrum fosters business agility by promoting key Agile values and principles, including:

items.definition: Understanding/prioritising customer needs, delivering value early/often, incorporating customer feedback.
Making decisions based on observation, experimentation, and evidence. Regularly inspecting and adapting processes to respond rapidly and optimise performance.
Delivering valuable product increments frequently. Enables quick response to market feedback, mitigation of risks, and adaptation to changes.
Formation of self-organizing, cross-functional teams with all necessary skills to deliver increments independently. Enables quick response to changing priorities without external dependencies.
Emphasising transparency, collaboration, and open communication within/across teams. Fosters trust and leverages collective intelligence.
Teams regularly reflecting on practices, identifying enhancements, and experimenting with new approaches. This iterative approach helps adaptation and performance optimization.

content.subtitle: Common Mistakes in Professional Scrum 🚫
content.description: By embracing Professional Scrum, organizations can enhance business agility, enabling them to innovate, respond to market changes, and deliver value more effectively/efficiently. Achieving business agility requires more than just adopting practices; it involves a cultural shift, mindset change, and continuous improvement. Some common mistakes hindering teams and organizations from fully enabling business agility with Professional Scrum:

items.term: Treating Agile as a Process, Not a Mindset 🧠
items.definition: Viewing frameworks solely as practices to be implemented instead of embracing underlying values and principles. Business agility requires a cultural shift.

items.term: Lack of Leadership Support and Engagement 👑
items.definition: Business agility relies on strong leadership support and active engagement. Leaders must champion values, empower teams, and remove impediments.
Implementing practices in isolation or inconsistently hinders business agility. A clear and consistent approach with standardized practices and continuous improvement is essential.

items.term: Resisting Change and Embracing Status Quo 🚫
items.definition: Resistance due to fear, reluctance to disrupt processes, or ingrained norms is a significant barrier. Overcoming requires effective change management, communication, and stakeholder engagement.

Micromanagement undermines autonomy, creativity, and trust, which are cornerstones of Agile teams. Organizations that micromanage or enforce command-and-control structures will struggle. Trusting teams fosters innovation and agility.

Business agility relies on a foundation of technical excellence. Neglecting practices like test automation, continuous integration, and refactoring leads to technical debt and reduced productivity/quality. Organizations must prioritize technical excellence.

Agile is about delivering value, not just features faster. Focusing solely on output metrics (velocity, story points) without considering outcomes or customer feedback may miss the mark. Prioritize valuable, high-quality solutions.

items.term: Lack of Continuous Learning and Improvement 📚
items.definition: Business agility requires a culture of continuous learning and improvement. Failing to embrace a growth mindset, solicit feedback, or reflect on practices hinders adaptation. Continuous learning is essential for optimizing processes, fostering innovation, and sustaining agility.

content.subtitle: Overview ℹ️
content.description: Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) is an Agile framework designed to scale Scrum principles and practices for larger organizations working on complex products. It was developed by Craig Larman and Bas Vodde based on their experience. LeSS is about applying the principles, elements, and purpose of Scrum in a large-scale context. It is more than principles and experiments; it also provides a framework with rules. The LeSS Rules define what is LeSS and provide a concrete framework. Within the framework, product groups can apply experiments. LeSS provides two different large-scale Scrum frameworks. Most scaling elements focus on directing teams' attention onto the whole product instead of "my part". Global and "end-to-end" focus are dominant problems to solve in scaling. The two frameworks, basically single-team Scrum scaled up, are:

items.definition: Up to eight teams (of eight people each).
Up to a few thousand people on one product.

content.subtitle: Scaling Challenges 🚧
content.description: Traditional sequential-lifecycle development doesn’t work well for small or large product development efforts. Agile development and Scrum have revolutionised software development, but scaling advice has often been unhelpful. Large scale product development isn't going away, so ways to do it well are needed. The concepts and principles behind Scrum, such as Transparency, Empirical Process Control, Iterative development, and Self-managing teams, are critical for scaling. Scrum hits the sweet spot between abstract principles and concrete practices. To keep Large-scale Scrum as Scrum, a similar balance is needed. LeSS aims to hit this sweet spot for large groups. LeSS needs to be simple when scaling, avoiding the tendency to add roles, artifacts, and processes. This should be avoided so that a process can be empirically created by the product group. Most other scaling frameworks provide a defined process, which LeSS aims to avoid. LeSS is Scrum Scaled: Instead of using Scrum as a building block, LeSS looks at each Scrum element and asks "Why is it there?" and "How can we achieve the same purpose on a larger scale with more than one team?". LeSS is scaled up instead of tailored down. Defining a universal framework and modifying it down doesn't work well, often leading to bloated processes because people assume everything is needed. LeSS should be kept to the minimum. LeSS Huge is separated out for larger contexts instead of "polluting" LeSS with optional elements.

items.definition: Emphasizes simplicity, striving to keep the framework lightweight and minimizing additional roles, artifacts, and ceremonies.
Extends Scrum, maintaining core elements (roles, ceremonies) to address challenges of scaling beyond single teams.

Multiple teams work from a single Product Backlog for the same product. Promotes alignment, transparency, and shared understanding. Product Owner manages and prioritizes in collaboration with stakeholders.
Encourages cross-functional feature teams responsible for delivering end-to-end features or components. Feature teams are self-organizing and autonomous with necessary skills.
Emphasizes mechanisms for alignment and coherence across teams. May include frequent synchronization (Sprint Reviews, Scrum of Scrums) and technical practices.

Incorporates Lean principles, emphasizing customer value, waste reduction, and continuous improvement. Encourages practices like minimising work in progress, optimizing flow, and maximizing value delivery.
Encourages flatter, more decentralized structure to support agility. May involve reducing hierarchy, empowering teams, and fostering collaboration/trust.
Promotes a culture where teams regularly reflect, identify improvements, and experiment. Iterative approach helps adaptation and performance optimization.
Based on transparency, inspection, and adaptation. Teams inspect progress, adapt plans, and strive for continuous improvement.
Strong focus on delivering value to customers. Decisions and activities are driven by meeting customer needs and delivering high-quality products.
Teams are self-organizing and cross-functional with skills to deliver valuable increments. Have autonomy to make decisions, plan work, and collaborate.
Promotes one Product Backlog for the entire product, shared by all teams. Promotes alignment, transparency, collaboration, and a unified view of priorities.
Encourages teams to be responsible for delivering end-to-end features/components. Minimizes dependencies and optimizes flow for quicker/more efficient value delivery.
Teams regularly reflect, identify improvements, and experiment. Helps teams adapt and optimize performance.

Incorporates Lean principles emphasizing customer value, waste reduction, and flow optimization. Encourages practices like minimising work in progress, optimizing cycle times, and maximizing value delivery.

Encourages teams to take a holistic view of the system. Considers interactions/dependencies between teams and the broader organizational context. Helps identify bottlenecks, optimize flow, and improve overall performance.

content.subtitle: LeSS Structure 🏗️
content.description: Adhering to these principles helps organizations effectively scale Agile with LeSS. LeSS structure maintains the basic structure of Scrum, extending elements for coordination. Team Organization: Recommends organizing multiple teams into one Product Owner team, one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done, and a common Sprint length. Teams remain autonomous and cross-functional, collaborating closely. Area Product Owners (APOs): In larger LeSS implementations (though not LeSS Huge specifically here), APOs may be introduced to help the Product Owner manage the backlog effectively where one PO cannot manage all items. APOs help maintain alignment within their areas. Structure the organization using real teams as the basic building block. Each team is self-managing, cross-functional, co-located, and long-lived. The majority are customer-focused feature teams. Scrum Masters are responsible for a well-working LeSS adoption. Their focus is on the Teams, Product Owner, organization, and development practices, not just one team. A Scrum Master is a dedicated full-time role. One Scrum Master can serve 1-3 teams. Managers are optional, but their role changes from day-to-day product work to improving the value-delivering capability of the product development system. Managers improve the system by practicing Go See, encouraging Stop & Fix, and promoting "experiments over conformance". For the product group, establish the complete LeSS structure "at the start". For the larger organization beyond the product group, adopt LeSS evolutionarily using Go and See to create an organization where experimentation and improvement is the norm.

content.subtitle: LeSS Product 📦
content.description: LeSS Product:

items.definition: Shared by all teams working on the product. Contains all features, enhancements, and technical items. Owned and prioritized by the Product Owner in collaboration with stakeholders.

Maintains a single DoD for the entire product for consistency and quality. Specifies criteria for a complete, potentially shippable product increment. Each team can have their own stronger DoD by expanding the common one. The perfection goal is to improve the DoD to result in a shippable product each Sprint or more frequently.

Product Owners collaborate closely for alignment, managing dependencies, and effective backlog prioritization. They work together to define vision, goals, and roadmap. There is one Product Owner and one Product Backlog for the complete shippable product. The PO is supported by multiple Teams working directly with customers/users and stakeholders for refinement. All prioritization goes through the PO, but clarification is directly between Teams and customers/users/stakeholders as much as possible.
The definition of product should be as broad and end-user/customer centric as practical. Over time, it might expand.

content.subtitle: LeSS Sprint 🏃‍♂️
content.description: LeSS Sprint:

items.definition: Recommends a common Sprint length across all teams (typically 2-4 weeks) for synchronization, predictability, and alignment. Shorter sprints are preferred for faster feedback and adaptation.

Teams collectively plan work from the Product Backlog. Collaborate to identify dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and ensure common understanding of goals/deliverables. Consists of two parts: Sprint Planning One: Common for all teams. Attended by the Product Owner and Teams or representatives. They tentatively select items for each team, identify collaboration opportunities, and clarify final questions. Sprint Planning Two: Usually done separately for each team. Teams decide how to do the selected items, involving design and creating their Sprint Backlogs. Can be done in a shared space for closely related items. Each team has its own Sprint Backlog.

A joint Sprint Review at the end of each Sprint to demonstrate the increment to stakeholders and gather feedback. Promotes transparency, collaboration, and shared learning. There is one product Sprint Review common for all teams. Ensure suitable stakeholders join.

Teams conduct joint Sprint Retrospectives to reflect on performance, identify improvement opportunities, and adjust processes. Focus on collaboration, eliminating impediments, and optimizing performance across teams. Each Team has their own Sprint Retrospective.
There is one product-level Sprint, not a different one for each Team. Each Team starts and ends the Sprint at the same time. Each Sprint results in an integrated whole product.

Cross-team coordination is decided by the teams. Prefer decentralized and informal coordination. Emphasize Just Talk and informal networks via communication in code, cross-team meetings, component mentors, travellers, scouts, and open spaces.
Product Backlog Refinement (PBR) is preferably done with multiple teams to increase shared learning and exploit coordination opportunities.

An Overall Retrospective is held after Team Retrospectives to discuss cross-team and system-wide issues and create improvement experiments. Attended by Product Owner, Scrum Masters, Team representatives, and managers (if any).

content.subtitle: Scrum of Scrums (SoS) 🤲
content.description: Scrum of Scrums (SoS) meetings are a coordination mechanism in large-scale Agile implementations where multiple teams work on the same product. The purpose is to facilitate communication, collaboration, and alignment between multiple Scrum teams. Composition: Typically involve representatives (often Scrum Master or team representative) from each team. Size and composition vary. Frequency: Typically held at regular intervals, usually daily or several times per week, depending on cadence and need. Can be adjusted. Objectives: Primary objective is communication and coordination. Provide a forum to share updates, discuss dependencies, identify impediments, and align priorities. Help ensure teams are aligned towards common goals. Agenda: Typically follow a structured agenda. Common items: updates, blockers, cross-team dependencies, coordinating upcoming work, resolving impediments. Agenda can be flexible. Facilitation: Facilitated by one attendee, often rotating. Facilitator guides discussion, ensures relevant topics are addressed, and keeps the meeting focused. Techniques like timeboxing, visual aids, and active listening may be used. Outputs: May include action items, decisions, and agreements. Teams may identify dependencies, impediments, and risks. Information and decisions help teams coordinate, address challenges, and deliver value. Scrum of Scrums meetings play a crucial role by promoting collaboration, alignment, and transparency. They help overcome challenges associated with scaling Agile and deliver value more efficiently.

content.subtitle: Daily Scrum Meeting ☕
content.description: The Daily Scrum Meeting generally co-occurs to discuss necessary tasks to reach the sprint goal. This informal meeting usually lasts 10-15 minutes. The scrum master must ensure it happens daily. It is not an extensive discussion and is also called 'daily stand-up'. The motive is to keep each team member in exact alignment. A work plan is made for the next 24 hours without compromising the goal. Team members usually focus on the three questions: What did I do yesterday? What do I plan to do today? Are there any obstacles?

content.subtitle: LeSS Huge Framework 🏭
content.description: LeSS Huge framework is an adaptation of LeSS for organizations with hundreds or thousands of people on a single product. It maintains core LeSS principles/practices with additional guidance/structures. LeSS Huge applies to products with "8+" teams. Avoid for smaller groups as it adds overhead and local optimizations. All LeSS rules apply to LeSS Huge unless stated otherwise. Each Requirement Area acts like the basic LeSS framework. The LeSS Huge framework is built upon LeSS principles but provides additional guidance/structures for larger implementations.

content.subtitle: LeSS Huge Structure, Product, and Sprint 🏢
content.description: LeSS Huge Structure, Product, and Sprint:

items.definition: The product is divided into Multiple Requirement Areas (MRAs) to manage large-scale efforts. Each MRA is a collection of related product features or components. Each MRA is managed by an Area Product Owner (APO) responsible for prioritizing backlog items within their area and coordinating with the overall Product Owner. Teams are organized into Feature Teams, responsible for delivering end-to-end features/components. Feature Teams are cross-functional and self-organizing. They may be further organized into component teams or sub-teams.

Follows the principle of having one Product Backlog for the entire product, shared by all teams. The Product Backlog contains all necessary items. The Product Backlog may be partitioned into Multiple Requirement Area Backlogs to manage large backlogs effectively. Each MRA Backlog corresponds to an MRA and is managed by the respective APO.

Recommends a common Sprint length across all teams. Sprint Planning: Teams collectively plan work from the Product Backlog, collaborating to identify dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and ensure common understanding. Sprint Review: All teams participate in a joint Sprint Review to demonstrate the increment and gather feedback. Promotes transparency, collaboration, and shared learning. Sprint Retrospective: Teams conduct joint Sprint Retrospectives to reflect, identify improvements, and adjust processes. Focus on enhancing collaboration, eliminating impediments, and optimizing performance. Coordination may involve regular synchronization events (LeSS Huge Requirement Area Backlog Refinement, LeSS Huge Product Backlog Refinement). Coordination may also include architectural/technical practices. LeSS Huge encourages incremental adoption, starting small and expanding gradually. Focus on establishing a strong foundation of Agile practices/principles before scaling. Adoption guided by continuous improvement. Incorporates Lean thinking and systems thinking to optimize flow, minimise waste, and enhance performance. Encourages Lean practices.

content.subtitle: Overview ℹ️
content.description: Fundamental information gathering skills are crucial within Agile methodologies as they ensure teams have necessary insights for informed decisions and effective adaptation. Data gathering is the process of preparing for and collecting data for project decision making. Data provides information on a specific topic, kept on record and used for decisions. It is important to understand the quality (accuracy, reliability, relevance) of the collected data. Some Information Gathering Skills include: Interviewing, Observation, and Brainstorming.

content.subtitle: Interviewing 🗣️
content.description: Interviewing: Purpose: Helps Agile teams gather firsthand information from stakeholders, users, or subject matter experts to understand perspectives, needs, and requirements. Techniques: Agile teams conduct structured interviews with open-ended questions. May use techniques like user story mapping interviews or stakeholder interviews. Benefits: Provides valuable insights into user needs, expectations, pain points, and priorities. Helps teams gain empathy and a deeper understanding of the problem domain. The interview is the most flexible and direct tool for eliciting requirements. It is also more prone to misunderstanding and failure. Interviewing stakeholders is an indispensable tool for verbal responses and observing nonverbal reactions (attitudes, body language, emotional overtones). These nonverbal connotations provide human context. The interview is a sensitive tool; its flexibility can lead to blind alleys. Interviews are limited by time and are a precious commodity requiring careful planning. Interviewing needs significant "people skill" and experience. Early interviews have a broad scope, while later ones focus on detail. To maximize benefits and control flow, the interviewer must construct the interview from building blocks with predefined scope and identifiable goals. Types of interview techniques: Unstructured interview, Structured interview, Semi structured interview.

content.subtitle: Observation 👀
content.description: Observation: Purpose: Involves directly observing users, stakeholders, or processes to gain insights into behaviours, interactions, and pain points. Techniques: Agile teams may conduct user observation sessions (observing users in their environment), shadowing, or ethnographic research. Benefits: Provides firsthand, real-time insights into user behaviours, preferences, and challenges. Helps teams identify usability issues, uncover hidden needs, and validate assumptions, leading to informed decision-making. Observation needs something that can be observed. Observation of individuals in teams leads to characteristics of an effective team member, such as understanding group goals, being friendly, confronting conflict, listening, including others, respecting differences, contributing ideas, valuing contributions, recognising team efforts, and encouraging feedback on team performance.

content.subtitle: Brainstorming 💡
content.description: Brainstorming: The term refers to group attempts to solve specific problems or develop new ideas by amassing spontaneous, unrestrained contributions. The technique separates suggestion of solutions from discussion of their value. The basic rule is no one can comment on or belittle another member's suggestion. Purpose: Foster creativity and generate a wide range of ideas or solutions. Techniques: Agile teams facilitate sessions where members share ideas openly. Techniques like mind mapping, affinity diagramming, or silent brainstorming may be used. Benefits: Encourages collaboration, diversity of thought, and innovation. Allows teams to explore different perspectives and generate potential solutions. Much value can be achieved by separating suggesting solutions from evaluating them. While useful for generating ideas, it's unrealistic to expect it to accomplish most problem-solving or planning tasks alone. It has value as part of a larger effort including individual idea generation, compilation, evaluation, and selection. Brainstorming can generate components of a plan, process, solution, or approach, and produce checklists. Major benefits: Encourages "out-of-the-box" thinking by challenging/inspiring participants. Full solutions can emerge from accumulating ideas, building upon proposals. Scope of solutions goes beyond individual group interests. Responsibilities of the conductor: Establish a professional/objective tone. Establish and enforce rules. Introduce goals and agenda. Manage the meeting and keep participants focused. Facilitate decision making/accord building, avoiding taking sides. Ensure all stakeholders have an equal chance to voice opinions. Control disruptive/unproductive behaviour.

content.subtitle: Overview ℹ️
content.description: Agile software development methods and proponents suggest ‘just enough’ documentation on agile projects.

content.subtitle: Types of Software Documentation 📑
content.description: Types of Software Documentation: All written documents and materials accompanying software. Divided into two categories:

items.definition: Records the progress of the development cycle. Materials created for tracking the project, passing/storing information, plans, estimates, etc., making the process visible. Visible processes enable more effective management. Types include project plans, test schedules, reports, standards, meeting notes, business correspondence.
Focuses on the developed software product. Offers descriptions/information and instructions on how to perform tasks. Includes: User documentation and System documentation.

content.subtitle: Documentation Practices ✍️
content.description: You must work closely with the customer for their documentation. Failure to do so risks creating too much, unnecessary, or documentation that doesn't meet actual needs. Agile documents are sufficiently accurate, consistent, and detailed. They do not need to be perfect; just good enough. Agile documents are sufficiently indexed. Documentation isn't effective if information cannot be easily found; an index and table of contents are important.

content.subtitle: Critical Points 🔍
content.description: Critical points about documentation:

items.definition: The fundamental issue is effective communication, not documentation.
Documentation is as much a part of the system as the source code.
You should actually need the documentation, not just want it.

The investment in system documentation is a business decision, not a technical one. Stakeholders decide, as it is their money. You may need to educate stakeholders about the importance of certain documentation.
The reader, not the writer, determines whether documentation is sufficient.
